lead: Hold one end of a metal rod in boiling water and the rest warms slowly, the sharpest temperature differences fading first. The one-dimensional heat equation describes this: the rate of change of temperature at a point is proportional to the curvature of the temperature profile there. It is used in heat-sink design, in cooling models for transformers and chips, and in finance under another name. This chapter solves it by separation, giving sine modes whose heights decay exponentially in time.
prereq: You need separation of variables from 5.3, second order ODEs from Unit 2, and later 5.7 for general initial data.

sections.h3: The rod, the diffusivity and the two ends

blocks.text: Take a thin rod along the x-axis, length L metres. Let u(x,t) be the temperature in °C at position x metres and time t seconds.

blocks.where: u<sub>t</sub> = ∂u/∂t is the rate of temperature change (°C/s); u<sub>xx</sub> = ∂²u/∂x² is the curvature of the profile; α² is the thermal diffusivity of the material in m²/s.

blocks.text: Here the diffusivity is written α²; some books write ut = α uxx and call α the diffusivity. This book follows 5.3, so α² carries the units m²/s and the value 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ m²/s for copper.
α² is a material property, not a speed. Copper has α² ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ m²/s; wood is roughly a thousand times smaller, which is why a wooden handle stays cool while a copper base spreads heat quickly.

The equation reads: a point under a hot hump (u<sub>xx</sub> < 0) cools, a point in a cold dip (u<sub>xx</sub> > 0) warms. Sharp corners have large curvature, so they smooth out first. That is the whole mechanism.

items: Fixed temperature (Dirichlet): u(0,t) = 0 means the end is held at 0 °C, say in an ice bath.
Insulated end (Neumann): u<sub>x</sub>(0,t) = 0. Heat flux is −k u<sub>x</sub>, so zero slope means no heat crosses.
Initial condition: u(x,0) = f(x), the starting profile in °C.

blocks.text: For the steady state, set u<sub>t</sub> = 0. Then u<sub>xx</sub> = 0, so u = Ax + B: a straight line joining the two end temperatures, reached only as t → ∞.

items: Assume u(x,t) = X(x)T(t), the product guess of 5.3.
Substitute: X T′ = α² X″ T, then divide by α² X T to get T′/(α²T) = X″/X.
The left side depends only on t and the right only on x, so both equal a constant, written −λ.
This splits into T′ = −λα²T and X″ = −λX.

blocks.text: Solve the x-equation first, because the ends impose conditions there. For zero ends X(0) = X(L) = 0, only λ > 0 gives a nonzero X.

blocks.where: λ<sub>n</sub> is the nth eigenvalue; L is the rod length in m; X<sub>n</sub> is the nth sine mode.
T<sub>n</sub> is the amplitude of mode n at time t; the exponent is in 1/s because α² (m²/s) times n²π²/L² (1/m²) gives 1/s.

blocks.text: For zero ends (u = 0 at both ends), the general solution is u(x,t) = Σ<sub>n=1</sub><sup>∞</sup> b<sub>n</sub> sin(nπx/L) e<sup>−α²n²π²t/L²</sup>
blocks.where: bn are Fourier coefficients fixed by u(x,0) = f(x); see 5.7.

blocks.text: Mode n fades n² times faster than mode 1. The slowest mode sets the clock: after time L²/(α²π²) the first mode has dropped to 1/e ≈ 0.37 of its start.
If both ends are insulated, the condition is X′ = 0 and the modes become cosines.

blocks.where: n = 0 is the constant mode; it never decays, so a fully insulated rod keeps its average temperature.

blocks.text: A rod of length L has its left end at T₁ and right end at T₂, both fixed for all time. The profile drifts to a straight line, and the leftover transient still obeys the heat equation.

items: Write u(x,t) = v(x) + w(x,t), steady part plus transient.
Solve v″ = 0 with v(0) = T₁, v(L) = T₂: v(x) = T₁ + (T₂ − T₁)x/L.
Then w<sub>t</sub> = α² w<sub>xx</sub> with w(0,t) = w(L,t) = 0 and w(x,0) = f(x) − v(x).
Solve w by sine modes; it decays to zero, so u → v.

blocks.text: Numbers: L = 1 m, T₁ = 0 °C, T₂ = 100 °C give v(x) = 100x °C, so the midpoint settles at 50 °C. The same split models a chip package, where boundary temperatures fix the steady part and switching creates the transient.

figure.caption: The starting profile 100 sin x °C on a rod of length L = π m, and the same rod at t = 1 s with α² = 1 m²/s. The shape is unchanged; only the height falls, to about 36.8 °C at the peak.

spec.aria: Two sine-shaped temperature profiles show the initial peak at 100 and a lower later profile after heat diffusion.

examples.question: Solve u<sub>t</sub> = u<sub>xx</sub> for 0 < x < π and t > 0, with u(0,t) = u(π,t) = 0 and u(x,0) = 100 sin x (temperature in °C). Find u(x,t) and the temperature at x = π/2 when t = 1 s.
steps: Here α² = 1 m²/s and L = π m. Try one mode, u = e<sup>−λt</sup> sin x; it already satisfies both ends because sin 0 = sin π = 0.
Differentiate: u<sub>t</sub> = −λ e<sup>−λt</sup> sin x, u<sub>x</sub> = e<sup>−λt</sup> cos x, u<sub>xx</sub> = −e<sup>−λt</sup> sin x.
Substitute: −λ e<sup>−λt</sup> sin x = 1 × (−e<sup>−λt</sup> sin x). Cancel e<sup>−λt</sup> sin x to get −λ = −1, so λ = 1.
So u = C e<sup>−t</sup> sin x. The initial condition u(x,0) = 100 sin x gives C = 100.
Cross-check with the general formula: L = π gives n²π²/L² = n², so mode n decays as e<sup>−n²t</sup>; here n = 1 and the decay is e<sup>−t</sup>.
examples.answer: u(x,t) = 100 e<sup>−t</sup> sin x °C, giving about 36.79 °C at the midpoint after 1 s.

traps: Writing u<sub>t</sub> = α u<sub>xx</sub> instead of α² u<sub>xx</sub>. Check units: α² u<sub>xx</sub> gives (m²/s)(°C/m²) = °C/s, while α u<sub>xx</sub> does not.
Dropping the n² in the decay exponent. Mode 3 fades nine times faster than mode 1, not three times.
Using sines when the ends are insulated. Zero slope needs cosines, plus the constant n = 0 mode that never decays.
Taking a negative separation constant. A negative λ makes T grow like e<sup>|λ|α²t</sup> and the temperature blows up.
Picking a negative eigenvalue because the ends are zero. Zero ends force λ = n²π²/L² with n ≥ 1, so every mode decays.

quiz.q: State the one-dimensional heat equation and give the SI unit of α².
quiz.a: u<sub>t</sub> = α² u<sub>xx</sub>, with α² in m²/s.

quiz.q: Why does a sharp corner in the temperature profile disappear fastest?
quiz.a: Because u<sub>t</sub> is proportional to u<sub>xx</sub>. A corner has large |u<sub>xx</sub>|, so the local rate of change is large and the corner smooths quickly.

quiz.q: Solve u<sub>t</sub> = u<sub>xx</sub> on 0 < x < π with zero ends and u(x,0) = 5 sin 3x.
quiz.a: Here n = 3 and λ = n² = 9, so u = 5 e<sup>−9t</sup> sin 3x °C.

quiz.q: A rod of length L = 1 m has α² = 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ m²/s and zero ends. Find the time for the first mode to fall to 1/e of its start.
Why do insulated ends need cosines rather than sines?
quiz.a: The condition is u<sub>x</sub> = 0 at both ends. cos(nπx/L) has zero slope at x = 0 and x = L, while sin(nπx/L) has maximum slope there.

quiz.q: Both ends of a rod are insulated. What is the limit of u(x,t) as t → ∞, and why?
quiz.a: The n = 0 cosine mode survives and all others decay, so the limit is the mean temperature (1/L)∫f dx, constant because no heat escapes.

quiz.q: A rod of length L has ends held at 0 °C and 100 °C. Write the steady state and the problem the transient must solve.
quiz.a: Steady state v = 100x/L. Transient: w<sub>t</sub> = α² w<sub>xx</sub>, w(0,t) = w(L,t) = 0, w(x,0) = f(x) − 100x/L.

beyond: Not for the exam. A change of variables turns the Black–Scholes equation of option pricing into this heat equation; with an imaginary coefficient it becomes the free Schrödinger equation of quantum mechanics. With a source term it models drug diffusion through tissue. Numerically it is usually solved by the Crank–Nicolson scheme, which stays stable for any time step. Image-generation models called diffusion models add noise and then run this smoothing backwards. Search 'Crank–Nicolson scheme', 'thermal diffusivity table' or 'Black–Scholes heat equation transformation' to go further.
